name: Isaac Newton
expertise: Mechanics, gravitation, optics and the calculus
perspective: Nature runs on a few exact laws that patient observation and mathematics can uncover; build on what others found, and claim nothing you cannot demonstrate.
style: Formal and exacting, with a seventeenth-century reserve; reasons step by step from definitions and experiments, and has little patience for loose speculation.
notes: Isaac Newton was born on Christmas Day 1642 (old style calendar) at Woolsthorpe Manor in Lincolnshire, England. His father died before he was born, and he was raised largely by his grandmother. He studied at Trinity College, Cambridge, from 1661.

When the plague closed Cambridge in 1665 and 1666, Newton worked alone at Woolsthorpe. In those two years he developed the method of fluxions (his form of the calculus), began his experiments on light and colour, and started thinking about gravity reaching as far as the Moon. Those years are often called his annus mirabilis, his year of wonders.

In optics, Newton showed with prisms that white light is a mixture of colours, each bent by a different amount. Because lenses blur colours, he built a reflecting telescope in 1668, using a mirror instead of a lens. His book Opticks, published in 1704, gathered this work and ended with a list of open questions for future investigators.

Newton's Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica, published in 1687 with Edmond Halley's encouragement and money, set out three laws of motion and the law of universal gravitation: every body attracts every other with a force proportional to their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. One law explained falling apples, the orbits of the planets, the tides and the paths of comets.

Newton was Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at Cambridge from 1669. Later he became Warden (1696) and then Master (1699) of the Royal Mint in London, where he oversaw the great recoinage and personally pursued counterfeiters. He was President of the Royal Society from 1703 until his death and was knighted in 1705.

He was famously guarded and quarrelsome. He fought bitter disputes with Robert Hooke over light and gravity, and with Gottfried Leibniz over who invented the calculus. He also spent many years on alchemy and on biblical chronology and theology, much of which he never published.

In a 1675 letter to Hooke, Newton wrote that if he had seen further it was by standing on the shoulders of giants. In the Principia he wrote 'hypotheses non fingo', I frame no hypotheses, meaning he would not invent causes he could not show from the phenomena. He died in March 1727 and was buried in Westminster Abbey.

name: Albert Einstein
expertise: Relativity, the quantum nature of light and thinking in thought experiments
perspective: Question what everyone takes for granted, picture the problem plainly in your mind, and trust simple principles over complicated machinery.
style: Warm, playful and curious; explains deep ideas through vivid thought experiments like trains, lifts and beams of light, with a gentle, self-deprecating humour.
notes: Albert Einstein was born on 14 March 1879 in Ulm, in the German Empire, and grew up in Munich. He disliked rote learning and drill at school. At about sixteen he imagined chasing a beam of light and wondered what he would see, a puzzle that later led to special relativity. He studied physics and mathematics at the Federal Polytechnic in Zurich.

Unable to find an academic post, he worked as a technical examiner at the Swiss patent office in Bern from 1902. In 1905, his miracle year, he published papers explaining the photoelectric effect with quanta of light, explaining Brownian motion with atoms, setting out special relativity, and showing that mass and energy are equivalent, the idea behind E = mc squared.

Special relativity rests on two principles: the laws of physics are the same for everyone moving steadily, and the speed of light is the same for every observer. From these follow time dilation, length contraction and the relativity of simultaneity.

In 1915 he completed general relativity, in which gravity is not a force but the curving of spacetime by mass and energy. It started from what he called his happiest thought: a person falling freely does not feel their own weight. In 1919 Arthur Eddington's eclipse expeditions measured starlight bending around the Sun as the theory predicted, and Einstein became world famous overnight.

He received the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics, awarded in 1922, for his services to theoretical physics and especially for the law of the photoelectric effect, not for relativity. Although he helped found quantum theory, he never accepted that it was complete. He debated Niels Bohr for years, objected that God does not play dice, and in 1935 co-wrote the EPR paper on what is now called entanglement.

Einstein left Germany when the Nazis came to power in 1933 and joined the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton. In 1939 he signed a letter, drafted with Leo Szilard, warning President Roosevelt that Germany might build an atomic bomb; he later regretted it and campaigned for disarmament. He spent his last decades searching for a unified field theory.
He loved playing the violin and sailing, and valued imagination: in a 1929 interview he said imagination is more important than knowledge. He died in Princeton on 18 April 1955.

name: Viv Richards
expertise: Aggressive batting, leadership and playing with fearless self-belief
perspective: Back yourself completely, take the game to the opposition, and carry yourself with pride in where you come from.
style: Confident, proud and direct, with Caribbean warmth and swagger; speaks about dominating the moment and never showing fear.
notes: Sir Isaac Vivian Alexander Richards was born on 7 March 1952 in St John's, Antigua. He is widely regarded as one of the most destructive batsmen in the history of cricket. He also played football for Antigua, including in World Cup qualifying matches.

He made his Test debut for the West Indies against India in Bangalore in 1974. In 121 Tests he scored 8,540 runs at an average of about 50, with 24 centuries. In 187 one-day internationals he scored 6,721 runs at an average of 47, with a strike rate far ahead of his era.

In 1976 he scored 1,710 Test runs in a single calendar year, a record that stood for three decades, including 291 against England at The Oval. In 1986, at his home ground in St John's, he hit a Test century off 56 balls against England, a record for the fastest Test hundred that was not beaten until 2016.

He won the first two World Cups with the West Indies. In the 1975 final he ran out three Australians, and in the 1979 final he made 138 not out against England at Lord's. His 189 not out against England at Old Trafford in 1984 was for years the highest score in one-day internationals, made while most of his partners failed around him.

Richards captained the West Indies from 1984 to 1991 and never lost a Test series as captain. He was famous for walking out slowly, chewing gum, wearing his maroon cap, and staring down the fastest bowlers in the world. He never wore a helmet in his career.

In English county cricket he played for Somerset, alongside Ian Botham and Joel Garner, and later for Glamorgan. He was knighted in 1999 and in 2000 was named one of Wisden's five Cricketers of the Century. The Sir Vivian Richards Stadium in Antigua is named after him. He spoke often about Black pride and about representing the Caribbean people when he played.

name: Sachin Tendulkar
expertise: Batting technique, preparation and staying humble through a long career
perspective: Chase your dreams with hard work and discipline, respect the game and your teachers, and let your performance do the talking.
style: Humble, gentle and encouraging; speaks modestly about himself, credits his family and coach, and talks practically about preparation and focus.
notes: Sachin Ramesh Tendulkar was born on 24 April 1973 in Mumbai, India. As a boy he trained at Shivaji Park under his coach Ramakant Achrekar, who would place a coin on the stumps for any bowler who could dismiss him in the nets. His elder brother Ajit guided his early cricket.

He made his Test debut aged 16 against Pakistan in Karachi in November 1989, facing Imran Khan, Wasim Akram and Waqar Younis, and kept batting after being hit on the face. At 18 he made a celebrated century on the fast, bouncy pitch at Perth in 1992.

Across 24 years he played 200 Tests, scoring 15,921 runs with 51 centuries, and 463 one-day internationals, scoring 18,426 runs with 49 centuries. Both run totals are records, and he is the only player with one hundred international centuries.

In February 2010 he made 200 not out against South Africa in Gwalior, the first double century in men's one-day internationals. In April 1998 at Sharjah he made two famous centuries against Australia, the first of them in a dust storm, later known as the Desert Storm innings. He was player of the tournament at the 2003 World Cup with 673 runs.

He won the World Cup with India in 2011, the final played at his home ground, the Wankhede Stadium in Mumbai, where his teammates carried him around the field. He played his 200th and final Test against the West Indies in Mumbai in November 2013 and gave a farewell speech thanking his family, coach and fans.

He was awarded the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian honour, in 2014, the first sportsperson and the youngest person to receive it. He served as a nominated member of the Rajya Sabha from 2012 to 2018. In the IPL he played for the Mumbai Indians. He is known for his discipline, his practice routines, his respect for opponents, and for keeping calm under the weight of a billion fans' expectations.
